description: We are a Melbourne-based team participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our team has skills in software engineering, UI/UX design, and business analytics. We are building NISAR Change Explorer, a web app that uses NASA satellite data to explore changes on Earth. We welcome collaboration and are looking for people interested in data science, GIS, satellite data, AI/ML, or web development.
summary: NISAR Change Explorer is a web app for the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge that lets anyone pick a place on Earth and two dates, and see how the ground there changed using real radar images from the new NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite. Radar sees through clouds and at night, but its images are hard for non-experts to read. Our app reads the actual NISAR data from NASA, builds a colour change map (blue = brighter echo, red = darker echo), finds hotspots, checks rain and soil moisture on both dates so weather is not mistaken for real change, and explains the result in plain language with a downloadable PDF report. This turns brand-new satellite data into something farmers, students, journalists and local officials can actually use to spot floods, land clearing, construction, crop changes and other surface change.
details:
What it does

NISAR Change Explorer shows how the Earth’s surface changed at any location between two dates, using L-band radar from NISAR. Users get:

  • a before/after radar comparison and a colour change map of a ~10 km area;
  • numbered hotspots where most pixels changed the same way, plus a 3×3 “where in the area” grid;
  • how much of the area changed and how many hectares got brighter or darker;
  • rainfall and soil moisture before each date (wet ground makes radar brighter);
  • a plain-language verdict, possible causes and how to check them;
  • a downloadable A4 PDF report.

How it works

  1. Find a place – search by name or click on the map.
  2. Find matching images – the app searches NASA’s Common Metadata Repository (CMR) for NISAR Level-2 GCOV products (Beta, Provisional and Validated releases) and groups them by orbit track, frame and pass direction, because only images taken from the same view line up pixel for pixel.
  3. Read only what is needed – the user picks Before and After dates. Using an Earthdata login, the backend streams just the small window around the location from each multi-gigabyte HDF5 file at the Alaska Satellite Facility, without downloading the whole file.
  4. Detect change – it converts the shared co-polarisation (HH, else VV) to decibels, smooths speckle noise with a box average and computes After minus Before. If the whole scene shifted evenly, hotspots are measured relative to that shift. Data-quality notes are added (for example, a warning for Beta products).
  5. Explain it – historical weather for both dates is added and the numbers are turned into a short report and a PDF.

Benefits

  • Makes free NASA radar data usable without remote-sensing training or GIS software.
  • Works through clouds and at night, where optical images fail – especially important during floods and storms.
  • The weather cross-check and plain-language caveats help users avoid wrong conclusions.

What we hope to achieve

Give communities, educators and decision-makers a simple tool to monitor floods, deforestation, agriculture, construction and land subsidence. Next steps: add NISAR GUNW interferograms to measure ground movement in millimetres, time-series views across many dates, and alerts for chosen areas.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI
  • Data processing and images: h5py, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, Matplotlib, Pillow
  • NASA data access: earthaccess, asf_search
  • Frontend: React, Leaflet
  • Hosting and collaboration: Render (custom domain novaralabs.earth), GitHub
